Dying Well
DY-ing WEL
noun phrase (theological concept)
From Old English dēgan (to die, to cease to live) and Old English wel (in a good or satisfactory manner, rightly). The phrase captures the medieval and Reformation-era concept of ars moriendi (the art of dying) — the conviction that death, like every other moment of human life, is to be met in a manner that is theologically informed, Christologically grounded, and covenantally faithful. The Reformed tradition inherited, purified, and deepened this conviction through the Puritans, who produced an extensive literature on the Christian preparation for death.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Dying well is the covenantal practice of meeting death as a redeemed saint, prepared by grace and grounded in the promises of the covenant God, so that the last enemy (1 Cor. 15:26) is faced with faith rather than despair, with hope rather than terror. The biblical pattern is set by the apostle Paul: “For to me, to live is Christ — and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21). This is not bravado but theology: for the believer, death is gain because it is departure to be “with Christ, which is very much better” (Phil. 1:23). Paul rehearses the same confidence in the face of his own approaching martyrdom: “I have fought the good fight. I have finished the race. I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4:7). The Psalmist walks through “the valley of the shadow of death” without fear, not because death is trivial but because the LORD is present: “Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me” (Ps. 23:4). Revelation 14:13 pronounces a blessing on the covenant dead: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.”

The Puritan tradition took dying well as a full-orbed discipline. Richard Baxter's Saints' Everlasting Rest, Jeremy Taylor's Holy Dying, and William Perkins' Salve for a Sicke Man — all instructed the believer to rehearse the promises of God, examine the evidences of grace, confess sin, make peace with enemies, and commit the soul to the Redeemer. The goal was not a painless death but a faithful one — a death in which the covenant held, the Mediator was trusted, and the soul departed in peace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defined dying as “expiring; passing from life; ending; perishing.” The phrase dying well adds the moral-theological qualifier: not merely expiring, but expiring in a manner befitting one who has lived under covenant grace and is now entering its fullness.

expand to see more

DYING, ppr. [from die.] Expiring; passing from life to death; perishing. The Christian dies to sin daily (Rom. 6:11) and prepares to die physically in hope of the resurrection.

WELL, adv. [Sax. wel.] In a proper or right manner; justly; rightly. Used of manner and quality of action, as in “he governed well,” “she prayed well” — implying that the act was performed as it ought to be.

DYING WELL: the theological conviction, developed through the medieval ars moriendi tradition and refined by the Reformers and Puritans, that the Christian must prepare for death as deliberately as for any other act of the Christian life, bringing Scripture, prayer, sacrament, and community to bear on the final hour.

The opposite of dying well is not dying badly (in pain or discomfort) but dying badly (without faith, without preparation, without the covenant promises, in despair or presumption). The Puritans were especially clear that sudden, unprepared death was the calamity — not prolonged suffering faced with grace.

William Perkins, Richard Baxter, Jeremy Taylor, and the whole Puritan school wrote extensively on the ars moriendi — not from morbidity but from the conviction that a good death is the culminating act of a covenantal life, the final confession that Christ is worth more than life itself.

Key Scripture

Phil. 1:21 — "For to me, to live is Christ — and to die is gain."

2 Tim. 4:7 — "I have fought the good fight. I have finished the race. I have kept the faith."

Ps. 23:4 — "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil; for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me."

Rev. 14:13 — "And I heard a voice from heaven, saying, “Write: ‘Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.’ ” “Yes,” says the Spirit, “so that they may rest from their labors — for their works follow with them.”"

Modern Corruption

Modernity has stripped death of its theological significance, replacing preparation for dying with avoidance of dying, and substituting the hospice movement's therapeutic categories for the church's covenantal ones.

expand to see more

The primary corruption of dying well in modern culture is the medicalization and avoidance of death. Death has been removed from the home, the family, and the church and placed in the hospital — a place where the goal is to postpone it by any medical means, and where dying is treated as a clinical failure rather than a covenantal passage. The result is a culture that has no theological vocabulary for death, no spiritual preparation for it, and enormous anxiety about it. The therapeutic hospice movement has moved some dying back to the home and family, but without the covenantal framework of the Puritans, hospice care remains grief management rather than dying well in the biblical sense. The church has largely abandoned its ancient ministry to the dying and left its members to face the last enemy without pastor, without Scripture, without the specific comfort of the covenant promises for those who die in Christ.

A second corruption is the prosperity gospel's implicit theology that death (especially early or painful death) represents a failure of faith — the believer who did not speak victory over the disease or claim the healing. This turns dying into a spiritual defeat and strips the dying saint of the biblical comfort that Paul's death was gain, Stephen's death was sleep (Acts 7:60), and the Revelation 14 saints are explicitly blessed. The recovery is to preach the theology of the dying saint: death for the believer is not defeat but graduation, not ending but beginning, not the last enemy unconquered but the last enemy swallowed up in the victory of the resurrected Christ (1 Cor. 15:54–57).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The concept of dying well draws together the Old and New Testament themes of faithful covenant death — the patriarch's blessing, the martyr's confession, and the apostle's departing confidence — into a single Reformed discipline of spiritual preparation.

expand to see more

Latin ars moriendi — the art of dying; a genre of Christian literature that arose in the 15th century (the first tract of this name dates to c. 1415) offering practical spiritual counsel for the dying and those caring for them; the genre was purified and reformed by the Puritans

Medieval church tradition: the ars moriendi texts addressed the five temptations of the dying (against faith, despair, impatience, spiritual pride, avarice) with corresponding theological consolations; the Puritans retained the structure but grounded it explicitly in covenant grace and Christ's imputed righteousness

Hebrew shalom (peace, wholeness, well-being at death) — the patriarchal ideal of dying “in peace” (Gen. 15:15) and being “gathered to one's people” (Gen. 25:8); the Old Testament pattern of a death that completes rather than interrupts the covenantal life

Greek koimaomai (κοιμάομαι) — to fall asleep; the New Testament word for the death of believers (1 Thess. 4:13; 1 Cor. 15:6,18,20); it implies restful waiting in expectation of resurrection, not annihilation or purgatorial suffering

Puritan literature: Richard Baxter's Saints' Everlasting Rest (1650), William Perkins' Salve for a Sicke Man (1595), and Jeremy Taylor's Holy Dying (1651) are the classic Reformed-and-Anglican texts of the dying-well tradition, each grounded in Scripture, covenant promise, and the certainty of resurrection

Usage

"Richard Baxter wrote Saints' Everlasting Rest while expecting his own imminent death — a composition that became one of the most widely read works of Puritan devotion precisely because it showed believers how to contemplate eternity with faith and with desire, not with terror."

"The Scottish Covenanters who faced execution on the scaffold in the Killing Times (1680s) became paradigmatic examples of dying well in the Reformed tradition: their final testimonies, collected in Patrick Walker's Biographia Presbyteriana, show men and women who had lived their theology long enough to die in it without flinching."

"John Newton's late life was marked by a deliberate theology of dying well: he continued preaching into his final decade despite blindness and frailty, declaring that he would not stop until he could no longer distinguish his Savior from his sin — a dying man's final witness to the grace that had carried him from slave-trader to herald of the gospel."
